speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware, I spent several hours yesterday with President Nixon in Washington. I should like to take a few moments of the time of the House to report on those meetings and on the discussions which took place concurrently between the Ministers of Finance and Industry, Trade and Commerce, with their officials, and the United States Secretaries of the Treasury and of Commerce and their officials.
One of the purposes of my visit was to seek reassurance from the President, and it can only come from him, that it is neither the intention nor the desire of the United States that the economy of Canada become so dependent upon the United States in terms of a deficit trading pattern that Canadians will inevitably lose independence of economic decisions. I stated to the President as candidly as I was able the concern which had been expressed in Canada, and indeed by some hon. members, with respect to the character of the U.S.-Canadian relationship. That concern was precipitated, of course, by the introduction on August 15 of the new United States economic policies, but it has been reflected increasingly in recent years by the continuing flow to Canada of American investment with its inherent advantages and disadvantages.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the warmth and the understanding with which President Nixon responded to my questions and the candid attitude which he revealed. He assured me that it was in the clear interests of the United States to have a Canadian neighbour not only independent both politically and economically but also one which was confident that the decisions and policies in each of these sectors would be taken by Canadians in their own interests, in defence of their own values, and in pursuit of their own goals.

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON
speechtext: The century-old desire of Canadians to benefit from our North American neighbourhood and to profit from our relations with the United States, while at the same time remaining Canadian to the degree and extent that we choose, was put to the President by me and accepted by him without hesitation or qualification.

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
We are a distinct country, we are a distinct people, and our remaining as such is, I was assured, in the interests of the United States and is a fundamental tenet of the foreign policies of that country as expressed by the Nixon administration.
I should add that the President was sensitive to the suggestion that his August 15 policies could be interpreted as evidence that the United States was unable to accept a Canada with a strong trading and current account position vis-a-vis the United States. This interpretation he could understand, but he stated to me forcefully that it was incorrect. I have not the slightest doubt, having spoken to him, that his interpretation is the correct one and will be borne out by events.

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON

speechtext:
If I may turn for a moment to the specific question of reforms in the monetary and trading practices of the world, the President and I agreed that no benefit would be gained by any short-sighted attempt on the part of any single country-the United States included-to gain immediate advantage. If the world trading nations and the international monetary community are unable to support with confidence whatever agreements are reached, then no progress will have been made. The same inherent instability and uncertainty which precipitated the August crisis will return, but with a viciousness not so far present because governments and the private sector will have lost confidence in their ability to come to grips with problems of this importance and this magnitude.
In short, Mr. Speaker, while the state of negotiations on specific points does not permit me to reveal to the House the precise state of play on any of the items which are understandably of interest to all hon. members, I am able to say that I have not the slightest doubt that those negotiations will be culminated soon, that the economic issues outstanding between Canada and the United States will be resolved, and that Canada will emerge in a healthier state. Much of the credit for progress in the process is due to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), and to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) for the skillful, tough and professional manner in which they have led the Canadian team of negotiators.

December 7, 1971
Prime Minister's Meeting in U.S.
I have emphasized in these remarks those parts of my discussion with the President which were directed to economic issues and to Canadian-American relations. I hasten to add, however, that we spent a good deal of time on broader international matters-on the tragedy which is now unfolding on the Indian subcontinent, on the steps which are being pursued in the United Nations to arrest the hostilities and create a measure of confidence that the grievances in that area can be redressed, and on East-West relations generally. In keeping with the President's desire to inform the major allies of the United States about his pending visits to the People's Republic of China and the Soviet Union, we talked of the initiatives taken by both Canada and the United States to lessen tension and contribute positively to an orderly international climate.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform hon. members that the President told me with what pleasure he and Mrs. Nixon were looking forward to their visit to Canada this spring.

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING WITH PRESIDENT NIXON IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me state that it will not surprise the Prime Minister to hear me say that I was very pleased he had this talk with the President of the United States. I am also very pleased that the Prime Minister has returned home reassured as to the essential good will of the President of the United States toward our country, and reassured too as to the intention and firm determination of the President of the United States to see our country develop in independence and in accordance with our own priorities. I am pleased too that the feelings of uncertainty the Prime Minister expressed publicly some time ago to the Canadian people as to the intentions of the President and the intentions of the American people toward Canada, his feelings of uncertainty about the basic attitudes that the President might have as to the role of Canada in North America and as to the direction that the Canadian economy should take in the future, have been relieved and that some of the general feeling of uncertainty is now eliminated in his own mind and presumably, as a result of his statement, in the minds of the Canadian people.
I had hoped, of course, that the Prime Minister would have taken steps some time ago to try to remove these uncertainties somewhat earlier than he has done, but I am pleased that this has happened.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unquestionably it should be emphasized that good relations between our two countries and a clear understanding between our two countries are very important to us. However, in addition to general assurances from the President of the United States as to his views about the relationships between our two countries and his firm resolve to respect our independence, political and economic, and to respect our decisions as to what course of action we might take-and I do not doubt their sincerity for a moment-surely we have to get down to specifics when the relationship between our two countries is so interdependent. It is the attitude and the response of the United States administration on specific issues that will really affect this country. It never occurred to me seriously that the United States had any desire to pursue policies intentionally designed to cripple this country. The question really is, what view does the United States administration have with regard to balance of trade and terms of trade? What view does the United States administration regard as consistent with its own interests? What view does the United States administration have as to when its actions might impinge upon the independence or autonomy of Canada? It is also important to us to know specifically how the administration regards the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the United States dollar. Are the views of the United States administration on this subject likely to impinge in any way upon our independence? These are matters upon which we will receive further enlightenment in due course.
I am pleased to hear the very optimistic statement made by the Prime Minister this afternoon as to the manner in which he believes these problems-presumably the value of our currency in relation to the United States dollar, the auto pact, the general attitude of the United States toward trading relationships, the balance of trade between our two countries, the attitude toward Canada manufacturing rather than being basically a supplier of raw materials to the United States-will be solved. It is these specific matters that we have to be concerned about, Mr. Speaker, in view of the high degree of interdependence between our two countries. While we are pleased to receive a general assurance as to the good and firm intentions of the United States, the question really is how the United States administration will interpret its interests and our interests on any particular matter.
In view of the degree of interdependence between our two countries it is my belief that we must not only have a statement of general intention, which we welcome, but we must also work out some guidelines between our two countries which will assure us in a specific way that decisions are not going to be taken unilaterally in Washington that could have a very detrimental effect upon our economy and its development. I realize such guidelines cannot be worked out in the course of a single visit. I do not expect that. I am glad the process has been started. I am pleased-I do not know what is going on with my hon. friends at the back on the other side, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps they would like me to attack the government. I am trying to be reasonably positive and constructive in light
December 7, 1971

of what I regard as a constructive move on the part of the Prime Minister.
I emphasize that as a Canadian, and my feeling is widely shared in many quarters of this House, I am concerned about the degree of interdependence between our two countries and the extent to which decisions taken in Washington can affect us. I consequently believe it is important for us to try to establish guidelines between our two countries for governing our behaviour toward each other which will at least reduce to a minimum the possibility of unilateral decisions being taken that can affect us very significantly. I repeat that one cannot expect this to be achieved in one visit. I am pleased that President Nixon is to come to Ottawa in the spring. I hope the Prime Minister will regard sympathetically the suggestion that the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States should meet frequently and regularly and that one of their objectives at least ought to be the achievement of significant and specific guidelines on how we are to behave toward each other.

Mr. Speaker, we were fortunate this morning to be able to hear the Rt. Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on the occasion of a press conference in Washington, state something like this: "The

Prime Minister of Canada and the President of United States have agreed that they should each guide their own political and economic destinies while respecting the freedom of the other."
Today, at the opening of the House, he is still using this most diplomatic phraseology which, in any event, will solve nothing and bring absolutely nothing to the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, there is one thing that will have to be said in the House one of these days, and it is that this government is a past master in creating artificial crises in order to manipulate more easily Canadian public opinion. For instance, There were an economic depression and an extremely high unemployment rate in Canada long before imposition of the American surcharge on imports. At that time, the government put the blame on the United States in an effort to disclaim responsibility, thus finding an excellent scapegoat.
Mr. Speaker, I shall remind hon. members on the other side of some statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in October last, and particularly in a newspaper article titled: "Benson anticipates danger of return to the glommy thirties."
People get scared and that's the way the government seeks to get them grovelling on all fours before Finance.
That is what they are trying to do to Canadian public opinion in order to make it forget the government's inefficiency and administrative fiasco.
And at the same time, our foreign policy is taking another direction. The government is opening friendly negotiations with socialist and communist countries. It is also allowing our relations with the United States to deteriorate. Indeed, without warning and at the cost of millions of dollars, the government is taking steps to give some impetus to our economy in order to impress Canadians; and those funds will be borrowed from the Americans or from other countries.
This artificial crisis in our relations with the United States has been entirely created to justify a rapprochement with communist countries. The Prime Minister has spent whole weeks in these countries, but only two hours in Washington. Today he comes back with empty hands. He says that good understanding has been restored, that all is well and yet, there is an increasingly persistent rumour-newspapers have reported it this morning-that Canada is about to purchase more weapons from the United States. However, the Canadian government boasts that it is working for peace.
This morning again, I heard-this is serious and I shall end on this-that Retail Credit of Atlanta, Georgia, in the United States is purchasing all Canadian credit offices and that so far those of Montreal, Winnipeg, Toronto, Vancouver and Regina have already been handed over to American interests, which means, to all intents and purposes, that from now on the Americans are going to decide about the financial situation of thousands of Canadians.
The right hon. Prime Minister said: We come back with the assurance that in the future we can freely orient our own economic and political destinies, and this with the respect of others.
December 7, 1971

Mr. Speaker, I say this is bluff. This is a put-up job by the government to make us forget their administrative failure, to make the Canadian people gobble up more easily communist socialism. We protest energetically against such dishonest tactics; the future will surely prove us right.
The problem will certainly not be solved by two hours' negotiations. If the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was so right in October, then today the Prime Minister is wrong. One or the other is lying and, to my mind, the last one who went over is.

Mr. Speaker, I ask leave under Standing Order 43 to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture announced a $150 million program which it appears he intends to proceed with without giving farm organizations, representatives of the farmers or, indeed, members of this House an opportunity to express their opinions. Having regard to the record of the government as far as farm legislative programs are concerned, it is imperative that this proposal be thoroughly debated and examined by the House and the standing committee. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight):
That the matter of the $150 million program announced by the Minister of Agriculture yesterday in Winnipeg be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture so that representatives of provincial governments, farm organizations and others may have an opportunity to express their views on the details of the program.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we, on this side of the House, look on the amendment proposed by the President of the Privy Council with a great deal of satisfaction for two reasons. First, it is encouraging to know that a government even as bullheaded and arrogant as this government can be persuaded finally to think that, possibly, it has been wrong. This is a major breakthrough and it gives us much satisfaction. The amendments also disprove many statements which members on the government side of the House have made on radio, television and in the press, as well as in the House.

I am not talking about leaks; that is another matter. Those hon. members have suggested that we are wasting time debating this bill because government experts have studied the bill and everything is fine. They have said that we are obstructing, and holding up the passage of legislation. We, on this side, have always held that legislation should not be put through simply because the government has proposed it, because Liberal government legislation is not, per se, good legislation. We have always made that point. Now, by bringing in these amendments, the government has proved the necessity and the value of debate in the functioning of a free Parliament. If any proof were needed that it is the function of the opposition to point out flaws in the legislation, the proof has been supplied by the government. We must point out that legislation is bad and let the people know what is happening. That is why we debate bills like this
December 7, 1971

one, and that is what parliament is all about. As I said, if any proof were needed of the value of Parliament and parliamentary functions, that proof is supplied by these amendments we have been asked to consider.
The opposition attacked this legislation from the beginning. As early as September 14, in the second reading debate, the Leader of the Opposition, in referring to these sections of the tax legislation, said that the co-operative and credit union movements must not be killed. They must not be crippled by hasty and ill conceived legislation and we, in the opposition, must make certain that this does not happen. Well, if we had listened to our friends opposite, we should not have discussed these particular sections of the bill. They told us that this was great legislation, that it has been studied by their experts, by civil servants who sit in ivory towers, read text books and draw up legislation, and that everything about the bill was fine. How much do these civil servants know about the world of farming and business? They do not know much about running businesses and, obviously, they did not appreciate the true function of the co-operative and credit union movements. If it had not been for the work of the opposition in this House, these sections would have been rushed through by the rubberstamp members on the other side. That is what they were told to do.
You know, it is amusing for members on this side to see how government supporters can swallow their own words. I remember that on the finance committee the government had a majority. The committee gave its rubberstamp approval to the co-op sections, as they were then drafted. When the bill came into the House, the opposition had a chance to point out the inequities in these particular sections. All the backbenchers on the government side, and I will exclude the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton and the hon. member for Ottawa West, because early in the debate they said that these sections were bad and should be changed, accepted the Liberal philosophy. They had been told to do so by the Minister of Finance, by the Prime Minister or by others in that party.
Suddenly, after the debate in Parliament made people aware of this bad legislation, we find the trained seals on the other side wanting to get into the act. Now, they are beginning to tell us what they think about the legislation. Why did they not speak up in committee and in the second reading debate? Why were they all, except the two hon. members to whom I referred, silent? Suddenly, however, they realize that something is wrong with the bill and they think that perhaps they had better get in on the act. If we have accomplished nothing else during the present session, we have at least proved the real value of parliamentary debate. The members on the other side, whose leaders seem to think that they run a sausage machine type of operation and that it would be a mistake to permit their supporters to speak their minds, are now speaking up. They were the people who were complaining most about the opposition wasting time in debating this bill in Parliament. I can only say to those people, if that time was wasted it was well wasted. We have amendments now that will correct a great deal-

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I wish to state that we support the amendments introduced yesterday by the President of the Privy Council. They are in line with the amendment I moved on November 18 on behalf of the members of the New Democratic Party. We are happy that the Minister of Finance has at last seen the light or had a change of heart. If this amendment is not the result of the minister seeing the light or having a change of heart, then someone else got to him and successfully twisted his arm.
It is important to note that this is an historic day for the co-operative and credit union movement in Canada. In fact, it has been said they are receiving a new charter. This is a new day for them, since a taxation provision which has been on the statute books of Canada for 25 years, one which can only be classified as discriminatory and iniquitous as it applied to co-operatives, has at last been repealed. It might be interesting to note that it is 25 years since the capital employed concept of taxing cooperatives was introduced. It was in the summer of 1946 when, following considerable study of the subject and after a good deal of pressure from organizations that I need not name at this moment, the government buckled and introduced a piece of legislation which set the stage for discrimination against the co-operative movement in Canada.
When this subject was debated in the summer of 1946, I had the opportunity of sitting in the gallery of this House of Commons and listening to some of the debate on the subject. I recall listening to Mr. T. J. Bentley, the late member for Swift Current, outlining the operation of co-operatives in a very simple fashion. It should have been very simple for anyone to understand but, even at that time, it was apparent that some members of the government had a great deal of difficulty understanding some of the elementary concepts involved. Later in the House of Commons, I listened to my late father, Mr. J. W. Burton, the member for Humboldt, speaking on this same subject. I took note of some of the remarks he made at that time, along with the late Mr. Bentley. One sentence my father used in the debate at that time is as relevant today as then. He made this statement, and I quote:
There is the other factor, the minister's attempt to force all cooperatives into paying a return on the invested capital. I ask: Where is their so-called free enterprise when they are forcing those who find good in the cooperative movement to accept their pagan philosophy that the wages of money must receive the first consideration? That is a vital question in so far as those of us who are in the cooperative movement are concerned.
That statement is as relevant today as when it was made on July 18, 1946, 25 years ago. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre was here at the time.

speechtext:
This subject was debated in committee of the whole on November 18 and 19. The discussion centred on the inequity involved in the government's proposals as contained in Bill C-259. I wish to place on record the fact that there were objections from both sides of the House. Members of the New Democratic Party were unequivocal in their stand. They made it clear they were opposed to the government's proposals as they were first put forward, and even to the later modifications, because those amounted simply to a change in degree, not to a change in principle. I moved an amendment to strike out the capital employed concept for taxing co-operatives. I noted that consequential amendments would be required to give effect to such a change and to introduce the alternative of a withholding tax as had been proposed by the co-operative movement and by the Co-operative Union of Canada in particular. The New Democratic Party was unanimous in its opposition to the proposals in the bill and in calling upon the government to accept the proposals which had been placed before it by the Co-operative Union of Canada. We are happy that at last the government has seen fit to accept those proposals.
It is interesting to note the changes which have been made in the government's position on this matter during the past year. In the white paper originally submitted late in 1969, it was proposed to retain the capital employment concept as applied to co-operatives and to extend it to the credit union movement, which was obviously ridiculous. In addition, it called for an increase in the level of capital employed which would be used to calculate the taxation of co-operatives and credit unions-there would be an increase from 3 per cent to 7 per cent. Objection was taken to this and the government thought it was responding by saying: Well, the old legislation fixed it at 3 per cent, the white paper said 7 per cent, so let us split the difference. The result will be a nice compromise. It is a question, Mr. Chairman, whether slow strangulation is preferable to quick strangulation. That is the only difference. Later, the government was forced to admit that its proposals were still not good enough.
The administration came up with a third proposal under which an option would be given to the co-operatives: they could be taxed at the lesser of the 5 per cent capital employed formula or one-third of taxable income in the way any normal corporation operates. This proposition, too, was unacceptable because it opened the door to further changes which might destroy the movement. Now, a fundamental change has been proposed and placed before the committee. We are happy that this change has been made by the government.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
I was particularly interested in one statement made by the President of the Privy Council when he introduced this new proposal yesterday afternoon. He said that rather than modify the old system, a system which was inappropriate to start with, the government would seek a new and more appropriate method which would recognize that a co-operative was a group of people who had organized to help themselves. I agree with that point of view. I took particular note of the comment "a system which was inappropriate to start with." It seems to me it is not a case of someone suddenly seeing the light.
Income Tax Act
This must have been known to some people in the government for a long time before the minister made his statement yesterday, and I can only conclude there must have been tremendous pressures on the government from behind the scenes which prevented them making such a necessary change before the minister made his statement yesterday.
The amendments which have been introduced recognize that co-operatives and credit unions are non profit-making institutions designed to provide a service to members at the lowest possible cost. The rule for taxation should be the proper taxation of refunds in the hands of recipients. The proposals now introduced do include coverage of two points which the co-operative and credit union movement has fully acknowledged. The first is that there should be full taxation of earnings by non-members. There is no question about this. Second, there should also be taxation of undistributed earnings. These are important points which need to be kept in mind. We are very happy with the provision for the taxation of patronage funds in the hands of recipients, taxation to be confined to refunds which are associated with the individual's business in earning a living; in other words, directly related to business rather than to consumer purchase.
As a result of these changes which, I am sure, will be approved, the co-operative and credit union movement is faced with a new challenge to do even more in our society than has been done in the past. Taxation impediments have now been removed. This opens the door to new opportunities for the movement. The co-operative and credit union movement has already made a significant contribution to the welfare of the Canadian people. It is also making a significant contribution on the international scene. In the developing countries of the world, the co-operative and credit union movement is considered an important tool in improving conditions and providing for a greater measure of equity between nations. There is a continuing role for the movement to play in Canada and on the world scene. New opportunities will emerge, new challenges will have to be faced. I certainly hope that both the co-operatives and the credit unions can accept these challenges and play the full role which they must play if we are to see a better Canada. They can make a significant contribution toward achieving greater equity among the Canadian people; and doing away with the injustices which have been so rife in our society. And, as I say, they can make a significant contribution to national development. All these things are part of the job which the movement must carry out. Now, let us get on with the job. The Parliament of Canada has gone a good deal in introducing and implementing these amendments as they affect the co-operative and the credit union movements.

had put in the wording of the bill for things to be mixed up that way. We wondered if the amendment would be read or moved. Some Liberal members yelled not to do anything nor talk about it. We simply had to read the amendment since there were only two days left. Two days! One day of debate in Parliament represents four hours only, and often much less. Which means that we have approximately seven or eight hours of debate left and then it will be said that the opposition carried on a filibuster for four, five or six days, which is absolutely untrue. I would like the Canadian people to know that a day in Parliament is not eight hours long, but more often lasts only two hours. We therefore have only seven hours to discuss that bill of 700 pages with amendments and subamendments covering over 300 pages and we will have to pass it, because we are now under closure.
Those amendments were read yesterday and I arrived here early this morning to examine them. Unfortunately, they have just been distributed to us which means it will be quite difficult for us to study them. All I read on the matter was the report published this morning in the newspaper Le Devoir and I quote:
New Amendments in favour of Co-operatives and Credit Unions
I object against those misleading headlines, especially since they refer to "amendments in favour of co-operatives and credit unions".
In order to encourage co-operatives and credit unions, the government should have left them as they are. I would have supported that but I am objecting now because we are destroying something that made no sense to replace it with something else that does not make much more sense either.
Mr. Chairman, I quote from the paper's article:

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS

speechtext:
The government leader in the House, Mr. Allan MacEachen, announced yesterday during the debate on the tax reform bill that the "employed capital" concept will be abandoned with regard to co-operatives.
Thus, the income of co-operatives resulting from business transacted with their members and which is distributed in the form of patronage dividends will not be taxed. The ceiling on admissible deductions for such patronage dividends will be removed.
As a substitute, the government has proposed that the patronage dividends be subject to a withholding tax of 15 per cent to be applied to any amount in excess of $100 paid to a member in a given year. The withholding tax collected will be reimbursable to the extent that it exceeds the amount of tax owed by the taxpayer.
Mr. MacEachen has indicated that those receiving patronage dividends will be treated as they were before, that is to say if the dividend is related to the business of the man receiving it, it will be included in his income for income tax purposes.
In the case of the small credit unions and the caisses populaires, the government has decided to tax their income at the rate of 25 per cent as long as their reserves exceeding those allowed under the Income Tax Act do not exceed by more than 5 per cent the deposits and capital stock.
In the opinion of Mr. MacEachen this special prerogative to use an effective taxe rate of 25 per cent on corporate income may well be insufficient for the small credit unions and the caisses populaires which would require reserves upward of 5 per cent to ensure there financial stability.

I will stop here Mr. Chairman, because the minister admits it may not be enough for small credit unions. But he does not give a darn about it. Small credit unions may disappear or keep on losing ground, he does not care. That is exactly what the government wants in proposing those amendments.
We have always stood by the principle that whenever obligations are imposed upon the caisses populaires, they should be granted at least the same benefits as others. If we compare the caisses populaires to the chartered banks and if, at the outset, we wish to tax them as much as chartered banks, they should get the same benefits as the chartered banks and should be able to create as much credit as those banks. If the caisses populaires could, whenever they have $6, lend $100, we would not have anything to say. The caisses populaires would then say that they can pay their taxes. But that is not what happens: it is even worse because the caisses populaires are not given the right to have hidden reserves like the ones the chartered banks have had for years. Those hidden reserves amount to one, two, three, four or five billion dollars. Chartered banks never paid and will never pay any tax on that. Nothing is said about it; small caisses populaires and credit unions have to pay, we try to collect a few cents from them, sparing the big shots who have everything for nothing and who are undermining our economy. And Canadians must pay for that.
Mr. Chairman, I have realized since I came to this House, that there are two ways of having a tax accepted. First of all, the government confronts us with an apparently inoffensive bill, but later progressively increases taxation each year or twice a year. In that way, it reaches its goal, which is taxation at the rate of 100 per cent. In the past, several governments resorted to such a method.
However, this government is using another strategy in order to have its proposed taxes accepted. It stuns its victim with white papers in which the 100 per cent tax rate is suggested. No doubt it was noted that each time a white paper is published, Canadians react with rage, precisely, because it proposes maximum taxation. After the first shock, hon. members consider the white paper, express criticism, point to the drawbacks and finally propose amendments. Therefore this means that opposition members have endorsed its principle whereas, at the outset, we simply stated that we rejected the principle of both the tax and the omnibus bill. In other words, most of the opposition members have accepted the principle once the first fight has been won. This is precisely the government's intention: have the taxation principle accepted so as to appear more conciliatory while reaching its original objective, namely the desired taxation level. I agree this is quite clever on the part of the senior officials who often spend three or four years studying the method they will use before tabling a bill in the House. This is how the government manages to have the House adopt as a lesser evil an unfair and unpopular tax.
The caisses populaires have accepted that as a lesser evil: instead of having their throat cut, they will have their hand cut. This government goes even further since it has the absolute majority. In order to disguise its indigestible measures, it invents omnibus bills like Bill C-259 with its
December 7, 1971

700 pages, not to mention the amendments that cover 300 additional pages.
Of course, the public will not be able to say that those thousands of top civil servants who are lavishly paid from our taxes are doing nothing. It is their job to cheat us in a clever manner and they manage to do that. The proof is that the majority of this House will carry Bill C-259 which will extort an additional $1.5 billion or more from our workers by resorting to closure. Again, whatever the minister might say, this notorious bill will enrich the treasury by more than $1.5 billion through taxes.
You can't work over such a long period on a bill seeking to extract a few more billion dollars without everyone noticing it. That is the purpose of the bill. Let us hope that the days of the "tax-happy people" are numbered. That is my heartfelt hope so that there may be a change of policy before our population is plunged into the blood-bath of a civil war mongered by the finance hawks who exercise a dictatorship over our country.
In the meantime, I tell government members: Tax away, go ahead, and hurry up before you are thrown out.
We of the Social Credit Party, who have long identified the real thieves of our vast national wealth, we tell the puppets of finance that their act has come to an end and our group was not taken in. That is why we have never recognized even the principle of this notorious omnibus bill. We have never accepted that monstruosity of a bill and we will vote against it. As for the caisses populaires, instead of cutting their throat they will cut their hand. We shall tolerate the amendments as a lesser evil but we will vote against the very principle of the bill.

speechtext:
It may well be that it is the role of the opposition, as he pointed out, to complain, and then if something useful is done to jump on the bandwagon and say, "Look, Canada, what we have done for you". It is unfortunate the hon. member is not here because I hate to speak about an hon. member who is absent. But be that as it may, I have rarely heard such negative nonsense as we were privileged to hear this afternoon from the hon. member for Moncton.
So far as these amendments are concerned, he attempted to create the impression that somehow the government and the House of Commons, all of us to whom he referred as trained seals, had no idea there was anything wrong until the Official Opposition pointed out to us that there should be a change made concerning co-operatives and credit unions. That was done, I suppose, to get some political Brownie points, to quote the distinguished hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and to convince at least the supporters of the opposition, who I understand are meeting this afternoon at the Chateau Laurier, that this was the case which it was not.
Income Tax Act
So far as co-operatives in particular are concerned- and I am not so familiar with credit unions-we have been subjected in recent weeks to one of the ablest lobbies that has ever been mounted since I have been a member of this House. I think the credit ought to go to the representatives of the co-operative movement, and I must refer to those I know best, in the province of Ontario, who were sufficiently responsible citizens to come here not for political gain or to create a lot of turmoil and get a lot of notice in the press, but rather with cogent and concise arguments. They came forward and said to many of us, "Look, I think you might take another look at these sections which are before you because we think changes ought to be made." They made their case well and, more than any other single factor are responsible for the results we see before us today. The hon. member for Essex explained this very well as he can so ably do. I wish to concur with what he said when he pointed out that the credit should go to the leaders of the co-operative movement.
There is another thing I am delighted to say which refers directly to the hon. member for Essex. All of us know that very few members are as diligent in pursuing things about which they feel strongly as is this particular member. One day, if changes were not made, he threatened to kick up a storm in this House, and elsewhere I presume, the like of which we had never seen and would never see again. We all know that the respected leader of the Official Opposition commands the name of "Big Thunder" in many circles in Canada, but I want to suggest to the House that even "Big Thunder" himself would be like a Pacific breeze in a tropical island compared to the tornado that could be kicked up by the hon. member for Essex if he so decided to do.
The point I am trying to make is that for the sake of peace, order and good government, if for no other reason, those of us on this side of the House who hold in awe and respect the hon. member for Essex had to work very hard to see if we could give him what he wanted. I think it is extremely important to note that the hon. member for Regina East points out that he has been asking for this sort of thing for a long time, too, and that his party is fully behind these amendments. When action such as this is taken, I suppose we should expect a lot of me-tooism. In a sense, I suppose, this is always the weakness of any government which attempts to listen to the people. Certainly, it is the weakness of the white paper technique of participatory democracy, because if you do listen to the people and do respond to what the people request there are always some political opportunists who will use that fact against you for political gain. However, I think we ought not to be disheartened by people like the hon. member for Regina East, but rather essentially ignore them and take seriously into consideration the fact that a good government ought to listen to people who have a case to make, as the co-operatives have done so ably, and then go on to take action which takes their position seriously.
It is for that reason of course that the government has decided to abandon the idea of capital employed. From this point forward, co-operatives will not be taxed on income from business which is distributed to members in the form of patronage dividends. I could go on, but all members are quite familiar with this. I want to conclude

December 7, 1971
Income Tax Act
by saying one other thing. I, like many other members, have had a good deal of correspondence on this subject. I want to take the time to read two short paragraphs from a letter which came to me from a Mr. Plewes of Carp, Ontario which read as follows:
Credit unions are non profit organizations which help low income people to borrow at reasonable rates. We need them today as we always have, more so indeed. The proposed tax will wipe out many credit unions, if you do not believe this you will have to prove it for yourselves, by which time it will be too late to right matters.
I am bringing this to your attention in the naive hope that you will see the truth of it and do something about it. I must say that it always seems to me an exercise in futility to write to a member of parliament about anything whatsoever, but hope springs eternal.
The point I want to make is that too few Canadians recognize the pressure they can bring to bear on the democratic process by putting their views forward to their representatives. I want this citizen to learn that his views have played a small part in effecting a big change. But we must all recognize that, in spite of the very negative attitude of the hon. member for Moncton, his obvious hostility toward what the government is and what it represents, in spite of the kind of position that he took even on an amendment that he wanted to approve, and in spite of the obvious political disadvantage of the kind of me-tooism represented by the hon. member for Regina East, this is a good government doing what a good government should do. We have introduced amendments which will help the co-operative movement in all parts of Canada, even in the riding that is represented, either capably or incapably as you wish to judge, by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville who is giving a mini-speech while remaining seated as I am addressing the Committee. I think the credit for what has happened must go to the co-operative movement, to the minister and his representatives, who were willing to listen to the representations that were made from many quarters. Among those who most ably made representations were the hon. member for Essex, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton and a great many others.

Whatever the weaknesses of this government are, it will never be criticized for being weak to the point of listening to the people, and no one will be able to say that more objectively and more enthusiastically than the thousands of members of co-operatives and credit union movements who have agonized over the utterly inept performance of this government in dealing with one of the economic keystones of our country.
We all agree this afternoon, government and opposition alike, because the government has finally come to its senses. The important question is not to score brownie points on the issue, whether it is the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton or anyone else, but to realize substantially what lies behind the days of debate that have taken place in the committee which would have been totally unnecessary had this government responded to the reasonable requests put forward not only last summer following the introduction of the taxation bill by the Minister of Finance but put forward months and years ahead of that and which were seemingly extremely sensible to all members except those on the government side.

Mr. Chairman, I don't really mind. A good speech always needs a little comic relief and the hon. member is providing that. It is obvious that it took the government some months to understand that there is something important about member participation in the co-op and credit union movement. It is obvious that that is such a basic principle that members on both sides of the House were willing to go to rather extreme lengths to preserve that principle, in the belief that failure to adhere to it in terms of our tax laws would ultimately destroy the co-op and credit union movement.
Much has been said in this chamber with respect to what would have happened had the government not taken the advice offered from all sides and by a variety of individuals. That principle has now been preserved, and we must be careful to prevent a possible future reversal through some further blunderous excursion, either by this government or any successor of it, which could destroy the unique contribution that is continuously made every day by the co-op and credit union movement.
I think it is important for the people of the country to realize that this House performs a very vital function in the democratic exercise in protecting their rights and privileges. In this instance, we have seen a clear example of the importance of debate on the dangerous changes that the government had advocated for so many months for co-ops and credit unions. Lamentably, Mr. Chairman, we are only a few hours away from the time when debate will be cut off on this bill, and I shudder to think of how many other areas, in terms of the taxation laws of the country, will be adversely affected by too little participation in this debate, both by members of the committee and by the public at large. I do not think one needs to be very much of a prophet to suggest, as I do, that in a very short period of time, perhaps early next year, we will be faced with another series of amendments to this major tax

We urged the Minister of Finance to go forward and score a touchdown, as the famous Calgary Stampeders did, rather than to fumble as the Toronto Argonauts did.
I urged the government to change the provisions in the Income Tax Act which taxed co-operatives and credit unions. I received many requests from my constituency that we should take a strong line on this and try and have these amendments made. Having supported the credit union movement as we have, I want to commend the government for these excellent amendments which encourage the supporters of the credit unions, the cooperatives and the caisses populaires. I feel that by encouraging the lending of money through these organizations in a responsible way to individuals who are often caught in emergency situations, we have assured an extraordinary measure of support for this kind of venture.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS

Mr. Chairman, as pointed out so aptly by my colleague for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), we may perhaps rejoice in the fact that the government has agreed at long last to lessen the disastrous effects of the famous Bill C-259, particularly with regard to the caisses populaires.
Indeed, the bill in its original form simply threatened to assassinate those institutions which have been, and still are a sort of backbone, especially in the province of Quebec. Caught and included in this heavy but lightly treated tax reform, the caisses had no choice but to insist with the members that at least amendments be moved to make some of the sections a bit more palatable. The amendments moved by the minister prove how right we were in criticizing those responsible as well as the bill itself.
There was no dely in debates, nor was there any filibustering from the opposition. We are rather confused by a thick, heavy, mixed up, incomprehensible and incoherent bill which embarrasses everybody, beginning with the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the ministers and their parliamentary secretaries.
December 7, 1971

Mr. Chairman, one is confused by a jumble of sections which are supposed to constitute a reform. When you say "reform", you generally mean "improvement"; if you change something, it is to better it, to make it more profitable for those concerned with it. But such is not the case, because the amendment which we are now considering means that the government itself has to redraft, bit by bit, its own legislation, and this, over a certain period of time, since the duration of the debate has been limited.
Mr. Chairman, it is important that the people know that the object of closure is "presumably" to accelerate the business of the House. I say "presumably", as closure was applied because the opposition was annoying or worrying the government. Obviously, that is completely false. Considering that each one of those sections requires a lot of consideration and study, how can the work be done rapidly? It is physically impossible, and the proof lies in the fact that section 137 has gone by the wayside.
Now, Mr. Chairman, If some sections are so badly written that they have to be completely revamped, we must say that in the 700 pages of the bill, dozens of clauses should also be modified.
That is why we feel that it was absolutely necessary to take all the time required to carry out the tax reform. It would have been easy-as many hon. members and many of my colleagues have repeatedly pointed out-to divide the bill in two and adopt immediately the sections that were not contested. There was no reason to submit a package bill that is badly written, incomprehensible and incoherent. But just the same, we must be happy that the government is nevertheless willing to lighten the much too heavy burden which the savings and credit unions have had to carry.
Mr. Chairman, this does not mean that in itself-as my colleague from Roberval said it so well-the reform is good. We do not want to help in the passing of legislation drawn up haphazardly, without any consideration being given to the views of the people.
In any case, this bill will be passed, whether it is good or bad. It must be admitted that when this bill was outlined in the White paper, the officers of Caisses populaires and co-operatives found out that high officials, or even the minister himself, had overlooked credit unions. If they had been forgotten at the time of the drafting of the bill, we must say that despite studies deemed to have been made and the publication of the white paper, a reform was considered much too soon. It is not that reform is not needed, as we of the Social Credit know very well-and we say so loud and clear-that there must be real economic reforms in order to get a proper financial and fiscal system. But to make reforms and speedily pass a tax measure for the sake of it, or to expect to go before voters at the next general election and be able to say that a certain thing has been done is illogical and most of all frustrating for the whole Canadian population.

Generally speaking, I think it is fair to say that all of us approve the amendments submitted yesterday by the government House leader. We are most relieved to be rid of these provisions as they were originally drafted, because they were most regressive. I think we ought to remember, however, that they had not been accepted by government supporters until the time the co-ops, credit unions and caisses populaires mounted their very, very effective lobby. My friend for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton complimented the credit unions and the co-ops on their most effective lobby. There has been much bantering back and forth-it seemed a little silly to me-about who should get the credit for the changes that the government finally saw fit to introduce. I will say nothing regarding credit. I opposed the restrictive regulations affecting co-ops right from the beginning. However,
I think it is fair to point out that the one thing we have discovered in this country is this: this government will respond to pressure. In that there is an object lesson for the rest of Canada. Canadians must remember that old adage, the squeaking wheel gets the grease. I compliment the co-ops on their very large, very active and totally justified lobby.
Having said that, I must bring up one other subject which members of this House ought to consider. What about the individual businessman? What about private owners of business? I have a message for them, and that message is coming through loud and clear. If private individuals and private businessmen want any consideration from this government, they will have to organize themselves as they were never organized before. They must do that to be heard. I am suggesting to the retail merchants, who in their submission asked for some parts of this bill to be deferred, that they had better beef-up their organization and make it as good as the organization behind the lobby of the co-ops.
Theoretically, no private business can compete with an efficiently run co-op. Yet, Mr. Chairman, they do compete and compete quite successfully. How is that, I wonder? Again, as I say, much has been said this afternoon about where the credit lies for causing the about-face of the government. That is not important, because the reason for the about-face is pretty apparent. The reason lies in the 2,373 co-ops in Canada with 1,690,000 members who are potential voters. That is the answer. The old power of the ballot box was suddenly felt. What about the other distasteful sections of the bill affecting those individuals in this country who are not organized?
I should like the parliamentary secretary to explain and make just a little clearer the effect of proposed section 135(7), as set out on page 10175 of Hansard for December 6, yesterday's Hansard. The proposed subsection reads in part:
(7) Where a payment pursuant to an allocation in proportion to patronage (other than an allocation in respect of consumer goods or services)-

Income Tax Act
This wording leaves me just a little bewildered. I am thinking of a very well run and effective co-op in my area. They have a feed mill, buy grain and do all manner of things. They run a retail department where farmers can buy farm supplies, fence posts, wire, hog waterers, cattle waterers, and all those things that are incidental to the successful operation of a farm. I wish to ask a question, and I know the parliamentary secretary will be able to answer it. I am a little concerned about what happens to patronage dividends in that particular area that are available to members of that co-op. Of course, I am delighted to see less red tape. The less red tape we have in this country, the better. I am all for that.
However, let me point out an anomaly in this area which fortifies my argument regarding the protection for the individual. Let us say that we have a customer who deals with a co-op. Let us say that he gets $99.99 worth of patronage dividend. There is no withholding tax, as I understand it, and there is no record or anything like that. Let us compare that situation with that pertaining to a poor, dear little old widow who has $200 in her savings account, on which the bank pays her 5 per cent. So, what happens? She gets a T4 income tax form for her income of $10 from that source.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent asked a couple of specific questions. First, the distinction between patronage dividends that consumer co-operatives issue and other types. Of course, the person who patronizes a co-operative store for his groceries is buying those goods with after tax dollars and any patronage dividend that he receives is a reduction in the price of those consumer goods and, accordingly, is not intended to be taxable. That is the reason for the distinction raised in section 135(7). This distinction exists in the present act as well.
Where the consumer is a farmer who buys binder twine, barbed wire and the other goods the hon. member mentioned, he is receiving a refund of payments he has made that he will presumably claim as business expenses as a result of his farming operation. The expenses that he claims must be reduced by the amount of the patronage dividend to determine his business income. Accordingly, the patronage dividend will be included in income in that case.
The fact that the withholding tax does not apply until the patronage dividends reach the $100 mark does not mean the patronage dividends are not taxable or that the amount should not be included in income. Co-operatives

will be required to issue slips, analogous to the ones the hon. member mentioned in connection with the poor little old lady and her savings account, to their patrons with regard to their patronage dividends, whether they amount to $100 or not and whether or not the withholding tax has been applied.
The onus is placed on the taxpayer to decide whether the type of business he does with the co-op is of a consumer nature and hence the rebate or patronage dividend is not an income item. Alternatively, if it is a patronage dividend with respect to business expenses he has claimed, the onus is on the taxpayer to report that as income. However, the fact that a withholding tax is not required until the $100 amount is reached does not affect the obligation of the co-operative to issue a statement to the taxpayer. That statement, of course, is verifiable by inspection by the Department of National Revenue. I do not think there is an unfairness here, as the hon. member suggested there might be.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the members of the New Democratic Party welcome the changes with regard to co-ops and credit unions. I will direct my remarks to credit unions because the hon. member for Regina East and the hon. member for Assiniboia have related their remarks to co-ops. That does not mean I have not been interested in co-ops. I have the honour of being a member of a consumer co-op in Toronto as well as a credit union. One of the reasons the consumer co-op failed in Toronto was the keen competition from the chain stores and some of their purchasing methods which denied co-ops certain buying privileges. Be that as it may, the co-ops have a very impressive record across the country, especially in the west. With regard to credit unions, I join with the many members in the House who have given credit to the co-ops and credit unions for the way they persuaded the government to bring about these changes.
One may ask, why the change? I can only relate my remarks to my experience while a member of the finance committee during the last Parliament. We were making changes to the Bank Act. I will always remember the tremendous persuasiveness of the banks with regard to taking the 6 per cent ceiling off loans. They were successful in doing it. One of their arguments was the intrusion of credit unions into the field of lending money to people across the country. There is quite a difference between a banking institution and a credit union. The philosophy of a credit union has been underlined many times. Its pur-
December 7, 1971

Income Tax Act
pose is not profit or charity, but service. I received many letters from credit unions in Toronto, particularly one which is called So-Use. It has a very impressive record of lending to new Canadians and has done well over the years. I quote from their letter of September 24, 1971:
New arrivals to Canada needed loans to establish themselves in this country; others were still paying their homes off, rehabilitating themselves after the depression and war. Lending institutions of all descriptions were demanding high securities and/or high interest rates, both of which were rather burdensome for most of the consumers. Therefore the Credit Unions flourished with the appealing slogans of low cost loans, loan and savings life insurance and mutual assistance for one another. Everybody felt like his brother's keeper. We had no direct access to the money from the Bank of Canada at the lowest rates of interest. We had to depend on the understanding and loyalty of our members. Warmth and confidence of our members to and in one another are the causative factors of our growth. It didn't just happen.
Those words are from one of the successful credit unions in Toronto. I wish to read the words of a credit union in my constituency. It is called the Woodgreen Credit Union Limited. In a letter to me, the president of that credit union said:
There are 92 credit unions in your riding. They all provide very worthwhile services to their members. I am in constant contact with their officers and believe me, John, only a half dozen out of 92 could survive.
He meant survive under the provisions the government originally introduced. When I think of the caisse populaire which have flourished in Quebec, I am impressed with the excellent record they have obtained. I wonder if conditions would not be much worse in Quebec if the caisse populaire had not filled the gap which banks and other financial institutions left through their failure to provide loans to people who did not have the necessary securities and credit rating that the banks demanded. I have heard it said many times that one of the reasons the credit unions are comparable to the banks is that they charge 1 per cent per month on the unpaid balance on loans. On the example of borrowing $1,200 at 1 per cent a month on the unpaid balance over a period of 12 months if $100 a month were repaid, the total sum paid in interest would be $78 and if you divide the $1200 borrowed by 78 the effective interest rate amounts to 6.5 per cent. Account must then be taken of the fact that the effective rate is likely to be even lower when the credit union declares its interest rebates to those who have borrowed money. Is it any wonder that the banks and other financial institutions put such strong pressure in the Finance Committee when changes were being made to the Bank Act? They realized that the fine motive of the credit unions was not profit or charity but service to the people.
I cannot avoid the conclusion that when the original provisions of this act were determined the government was corporation-oriented; it had been directly influenced by the large corporations, the banks and the financial institutions. Otherwise it would not have brought down the provisions which are contained in Bill C-259. Who would have thought of the capital employed concept which the Minister of Finance attempted to apply, not only to the co-operatives but to the credit unions? It certainly was not dreamed up after consultation with the credit unions. It was certainly arrived at after pressure from banking and other financial institutions.
I give very little credit to the government for bringing in these amendments. We welcome them, but I do not give them credit. In the first instance, the minister and his colleagues were influenced totally by the corporations. It was only after members from all parties had spoken out against the proposals that the government yielded. Incidentally, I found it passing strange that during the discussion of the personal exemption rates, the changes from $1,000 to $1,500 in the case of single persons and from $2,000 to $2,850 in the case of married couples, very few supporters of the government pointed out that 20 per cent of all Canadians would still be living below the poverty line. I am disturbed that supporters of the Liberal party did not rise on other sections and allow their voices to be heard in favour of necessary changes. I notice the parliamentary secretary giving me a slight smile. I can recall that when we were discussing the expenses to be allowed to workers there was a cemetery-like silence from the benches opposite, and that no criticism was levelled against the bill when we were discussing the expense accounts which are to be allowed to members of the boards of corporations in connection with their business.
We have a proud history in Canada in connection with credit unions. Back in 1900 Alphonse Desjardins of Levis, Quebec, began the credit union movement in Canada. From that humble beginning credit unions have spread across the country and served a most useful purpose. It disturbs me that the government should have brought forward provisions which would have strangled the growth of the movement. It took the efforts of members of all parties to persuade the administration of the necessity of credit unions and of their social usefulness. The argument which the credit unions put forward respecting the necessity for statutory provisions relating to reserves, the argument in support of their inability to distribute reserves to their members in the same way as corporations distribute their reserves to shareholders must have had some impact upon the government, because the changes made in the legislation reflect this point of view.
I trust that never again will the government be persuaded by the banks and financial institutions that credit unions do not play a vital part in improving the living conditions of most Canadians. When I read the statement by the Prime Minister, the remarks he made on National Credit Union Day, I realize he was setting forth the true philosophy of the credit unions. He said, then:
Credit unions have experienced enormous success because they encourage both regular savings and the wise use of credit. But even more important, credit unionism encourages self help, mutual assistance, and personal involvement. In this sense credit unions are more than financial institutions, they are a positive social force within our communities.
I hope the other members of the cabinet will take to heart the message the Prime Minister sent to all Canadians and never again be persuaded by the corporate interests of this country to bring forward such proposals as they first brought forward in Bill C-259. If they do that we shall succeed as we have never succeeded before in bringing about some of the social improvements which are necessary in this country.

December 7, 1971
Income Tax Act
