speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we have just heard the praise which the hon. member for Broadview has rightly heaped upon the Prime Minister. As one who has been associated very closely with many cabinet ministers, I should like to assure the hon. member for Broadview that the cabinet ministers do strive very hard to emulate the Prime Minister in that regard.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
I have been a member since its inception, 26 years ago, of the St. Stanislaus Credit Union, the largest in Ontario, with more than 12,000 members with its headquarters in Parkdale. I, too, was pleased to make representations in this House in favour of appropriate amendments to Bill C-259, and today I wish to express to the Minister of Finance, to his parliamentary secretary and to their officials, the appreciation of all credit union members in Canada for their patience and understanding in drafting the amendments which were announced yesterday. As hon. members know, the income of credit unions and caisses populaires will now be taxed at the rate of 25 per cent as long as reserves in excess of those allowed against income do not exceed 5 per cent of deposits and share capital. A further amendment will also mark the abandonment of the notion of capital employed and embodies the proposal that the limit on interest rebates related to capital employed be deleted. These amendments will go a long way to enabling credit unions to grow and assist their members, and, consequently, to further the growth of the Canadian economy.
I should also like to take this opportunity to pay a tribute to the credit union movement which has rendered assistance to numerous immigrants, especially in helping them to procure loans to buy houses. This is a great service indeed. For some reason or other, these immigrants have found it much easier to get a loan for a home from the credit union than from other sources. I am delighted to join the hon. member for Essex and my other colleagues in the House in expressing once again to the Minister of Finance our appreciation and also to congratulate the credit union representatives who have presented their case to us in a very reasonable, courteous and effective manner. We have seen participatory democracy work and succeed.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to point out that we support the amendments proposed by the government House leader to sections 57, 58, 135 and 137 which deal particularly with co-operatives and credit unions.
I am very happy that the representations of the co-operatives and credit unions and the reiterated requests of hon. members of all parties have been heeded.
As for us, of the Social Credit party, I know that we have not been very soft on the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when we asked that the sections I have just mentioned be amended. This is why I reiterate our appreciation for the proposed amendments. These are amendments which I think are much more equitable that the initial proposals. It seems to me follow-

ing the talks my colleagues have had in these amendments.
Everyone will try to interpret the tabling of amendments in their own way. Some will say that the government has taken a backward step, others that it has made a gain. I myself consider that the amendments to the clauses concerning co-operatives and credit unions are the result of numerous negotiations and pressures exercised by those organizations which stated their views in an intelligent manner but without kicking up a shindy. It therefore proves that it is possible to obtain results from a government when the people exercise the right amount of pressure and make themselves heard.
However, people should be in a position to make themselves heard. The government follows too easily the advice of officials who tend to try and settle problems with over-simple methods, without paying too much attention to justice. Our agreement to the amendments brought forward in regard to co-operatives and credit unions does not mean that we approve the bill as a whole. The latter contains a lot of nonsense, such as the inequitable way in which it sought to deal with credit unions and co-operatives. Several other amendments would therefore be in order.
The concept of capital utilized which has been incorporated in the Income Tax Act for the past 23 years, and which was the basis for taxing co-operatives, is a striking instance of the errors and inequities contained in the bill before us. I am happy that representations made to the minister have succeeded in moving him to bring forward amendments to correct an inequity which was about to be sanctioned.
Co-operatives and caisses populaires will now know what they are faced with. They are faced with a new challenge: that of taking a greater part in the Canadian economy and of having their members participate in the many services which they provide for five million people.
The co-operative movement is still new in Canada. In fact, it is only starting, after groping its way for a long time. I think that it has acquired valuable experience during those last few weeks' discussions and will be in a position to take up the challenge.
I do not intend to retrace the history of the co-operative movement in Canada, as others have done so before me- with great competence. I am glad of the turn events have taken and I hope this will serve as a lesson not only to members of co-operatives and caisses populaires, but to all Canadians.
That is a striking example which shows that solutions can be found when there is the will to talk business seriously. This is an important lesson for the government which will have to pay more attention to the wishes of the people.
In the course of the debates ahead further amendments to this bill will be introduced and I hope that the minister will welcome those proposals.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the significance of these changes to the bill. The government has moved from a substantial widening of the capital employed formula on which it taxed co-operatives
December 7, 1971

to a complete elimination of it. This is a change that goes further than most of us expected, but which I think is basic to the co-operative movement. The capital employed formula did not seem to have much basis in fact; it was a formula that was made use of during wartime in order to replace the excess profits tax. We are now returning to a straight 15 per cent withholding tax. The capital employed formula was a very poor way of taxing co-operatives, and as I say it is significant that this formula has now been changed.
I should like to make some comments on the effect of this proposed change on the western grain handling companies, which are divided roughly into three groups. There are the three western pools; the United Grain Growers, which operates under a somewhat different structure but is still to some extent a co-operative; and the private line elevator companies. It is significant that this change is made at this time because the grain handling system in western Canada is being reorganized. Even though the United Grain Growers has been in operation for 60 years and the pools have been operating for 40 years, the line elevator companies are still able to get between 30 and 40 per cent of the grain that passes through the system each year, in spite of the fact that in general I think they are at a disadvantage to their competitors, particularly the pools.
The elimination of the capital employed formula should substantially increase the competitiveness of the pools, and to some extent the United Grain Growers, vis-a-vis the line elevator companies. Whether this will see the growth of a monopoly in this area remains to be seen, but I think it is a definite possibility. We must wait and see how these changes to the corporation tax affect the value of this tax as a means of raising money.
We have seen a downgrading of the corporation tax in the last few years. The 7 per cent reduction mentioned by the Minister of Finance a few weeks ago and the dropping of the 1 per cent corporation tax each year for four years means that the government is moving away from corporation tax as a means of raising money for the treasury and is placing more emphasis on income tax. These changes with respect to co-operatives should further increase the revenue of the government through personal income tax. So I believe we must look at these changes to see if the corporation tax is to be reduced significantly over the years in line with the amendments in respect of co-operatives. If not, there may well be significant changes in our economic structure particularly in rural areas involving producer co-operatives.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, like some other hon. members I wish to commend the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary for bringing in the amendments they did yesterday. I can assure them that in a constituency like mine, which has dozens of small and large co-operatives, this is most welcome. The fact that the government has moved on this issue is a credit to the Parliament of Canada, as is the fact that members of this House realized that co-operatives would be strangled by this bill and have been able to convince the powers that be that changes ought to be made.
Income Tax Act
The New Democratic Party, as everyone knows, was committed to fight as hard as it could to change the mind of the government. I am very pleased that the Minister of Finance and the government have recognized this. I know also that many members of the Liberal party, particularly the hon. member for Essex, made their intentions very clear and because of this the government changed its mind.
More important, however, I believe is the fact that the co-operative movement itself deserves credit for the changes before us. I think we should all congratulate them for the tremendous job they did in articulating their cause and in convincing members who had not been convinced about the reason co-operatives exist and why this bill as first presented would have been very injurious to them. They should be complimented at the national and local levels.
I received 50 or 60 telegrams, letters and resolutions from co-operatives in my constituency, wheat pools and credit unions. I congratulate these people for coming forward and persuading the government it should change the legislation as originally presented to the House. In a democratic system I believe government should listen to the people and be flexible enough to amend legislation to coincide with the wishes of any sector of our society.
I believe all of us felt that if the bill had gone through in its original form it would have eventually strangled the co-operative movement. I think it is essential that government recognize that co-operatives served a very significant purpose in the history of this country. This is particularly true in a province such as Saskatchewan where the co-operative movement is a vital part of the way of life. Co-operatives are an integral part of the community. Back in the thirties when the farmers faced the great depression they had to band together by forming co-operatives in order to protect themselves from corporate businesses which did not care about them. In every town and village across the province of Saskatchewan hundreds of people are active at the grassroots level in co-operatives, not as a profit-making venture but as a service to themselves, to their families and their communities. This is the type of thing I believe should be encouraged in Canadian life.
I think we should note that our party, in 1945, in Saskatchewan about a year after it formed the government established the first department of co-operation in history and appointed a minister of co-operation. This is the type of leadership we should have in all parts of Canada. As I have said before, the co-operative movement is not a profit-making operation but, as the hon. member for Broadview pointed out, is a movement controlled by the people who use the co-operatives. You have one member with one vote, and not a few directors sitting on a board in some smoke-filled room behind closed doors making decisions which affect the people.
This is the direction in which we should be moving and I am thankful the President of the Privy Council presented these amendments. I hope they will stay with us in the years ahead because they will be of great benefit to the co-operative movement. I appreciate, as do my constituents, this step in the right direction in the decision of the government in amending the original bill.

December 7, 1971
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say this afternoon. They are not particularly weighty or well thought-out. I am very pleased to hear the tenor of the remarks of all hon. members who have spoken. They all agree, as I do, that it is a great thing to see these amendments and the changes made, since the future of co-operatives and credit unions is assured because of them. I certainly agree with the hon. member for Essex who first brought out the idea which has been repeated by other hon. members, that those who should be given credit for this are the credit unions themselves who did an excellent job in a very legitimate lobby. I would say this is a classic example, of which opposition members are not always aware or willing to recognize, that in a democracy if a story is told clearly, logically and cogently to enough Members of Parliament, people will change their mind and take a slightly different course in order to accommodate them. That is what Parliament is supposed to be all about.
I am very pleased that in this aspect we are proving, as we have at other times, that Parliament does have life and is not dominated by a bunch of dictatorial technocrats. This is the language of members of the opposition.
This procedure has shown that we have a future as a democratic state and that Parliament has an important place in a democratic state. We did not have television cameras in the House this afternoon. I am opposed to their being here because I think we do enough grandstanding without being encouraged to do more television. If the Canadian people were to have seen the great workings of this democratic, this almost sacred institution, this afternoon what would they have seen? They would have seen everybody agreeing to amendments to a bill, which shows the good sense of hon. members. Also they would have seen everybody here doing something that nobody in Canada can understand. They would have seen members wasting a whole afternoon saying, "You should have done it sooner," or "I was the guy who suggested it," or "It was me too"-a whole bunch of extraneous garbage which has nothing to do with the fact that Parliament has changed its mind and is passing a constructive measure. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said a while ago, for grown men to be fighting over Brownie points all the time is not something that the people of Canada find very stimulating.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: Then why are you on your feet?

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: This afternoon we have wasted a lot of time.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: Then why don't you sit down?

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
I wish that some members who most need instruction would listen to a little instruction from time to time. I suppose the fact that there are so few Conservatives in the chamber makes them want to make a great deal of noise. There are only four here now and the rest are away, thinking about how they will save the nation. I have not yet seen any blood on the street in front of the Chateau Laurier, but I think there must be some by now because they have been meeting for a day and a half.
The ghoulish glee that people have been expressing all afternoon, seeing that there is a time limitation on this

important bill, is a waste of time. Everybody on the opposition side says that time limitation is a crime and that they should be able to talk forever on this important subject. Yet we have four days during which to talk on it and we waste all one afternoon hearing people say, "I should get the Brownie points, not you". Surely we should have spent our time talking about other things. Great screams were heard last week when we said the time had come to pass this bill. But we have spent all afternoon listening to nothing more than ghoulish glee from hon. members on the opposite side.
After a perfectly legitimate process of tax investigation has been completed, we should now get on with the legislation. I should like to know whether members of the opposition are seriously preparing, when this tax measure is out of the way, to give us their views on poverty, on a guaranteed annual income and on how we are to attack our other problems. The fact is that all the old problems of regional disparity have not yet been solved in Canada's 100 years of existence and these are problems to which this government, and indeed any other government, must address itself.
Another matter for discussion is the development of trade on the Pacific rim, which our Prime Minister foresaw was the next big springboard for this country and which he has helped to encourage. Some people, in their ignorance, accuse him of taking off and flying all over the world. It so happens that when he flies all over the world we get an order for something, and if we do not have an order we will not eat.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: You have an order-the 10 per cent surcharge.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: That is enough from you. What we should hear is some truth and logic. You do not sell to the Japanese without making friends with them. You do not trade with emerging countries such as Malaysia without talking to them. You do not get anywhere without developing relationships so that people get to understand and trust you. Because we are the biggest trading nation, per capita, in the world, someone must do these things. But instead of members of the opposition coming forth with their viewpoints on how trade should be developing, they go around with whispering campaigns like a bunch of schoolboys. They say that the Prime Minister is out of the country too much.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: Why don't you read what our leader said as reported in the newspapers?

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
That is another thing that is pitiful-Brownie points made with newspaper columns. We take our responsibility of trying to run this country under the mandate that has been given to us. We are not afraid to find newspapers sometimes a little behind us. We do not look over our shoulders all the time, nor do we ask some guy whether we could vet the particular thing he is writing, and please will he make it nice. What we are trying to do is to get things done. We have developed more trade than any other government. We have sold more wheat to more people than any other government, and we have employed more people than any other government. But all we get from you people is raspberries and screaming all afternoon.
December 7, 1971

I will not be too long, Mr. Chairman, because it is obviously useless to waste any further time of Parliament trying to put fresh ideas into their heads. As I said, trade development is important. Let us hear some views on that matter when this tax measure is passed. It is almost passed now. Ten years have come to an end and the country is ready to go on to the next task, but all the opposition is doing is bellyaching about the fact that it is too bad that an amendment regarding co-operatives was not put in by one guy instead of another guy. That is real statesmanship!
The problem of the native peoples is a very difficult one which I do not suppose any of us understands as well as he could. But, by God, this government has tried to advance the lot of the native peoples as no other government has. It has a lot to learn and it has to grope its way ahead. It would be great if you people helped us.

speechtext: We will.

speechtext: Another matter is international relations. Instead of complaining that we are not friendly enough with the Americans, or we are too friendly with the U.S.S.R., or some other damn thing ad infinitum-

speechtext: You said that.

I said, instead of complaining give us your views about what international relations should be. All we have heard all afternoon is talk on one point, namely, who should or should not have brought in an amendment to a particular section in the tax bill which is 700 pages long. I have been listening very hard and that is all I got out of it. The hon. member for Dauphin was most constructive, but he was speaking in the past so that it was educational without advancing an argument. However, he spoke very intelligently and I learned a lot from him.
But the main point is that this sort of procedure, as I said, is not a tragedy for either a Liberal or a Conservative government, or indeed an NDP or a Social Credit government if there ever should be such an animal. The tragedy, which nobody here seems to understand, is that if we had television here this afternoon the people of Canada would completely lose their faith in the parliamentary system, and then where would we be? There is no way in which the people of Canada will buy this kind of stalling and fiddling about. They do not understand it.
The one thing I have heard for weeks is, why the devil have we not applied time allocation since we have a majority? We are asked why we do not get on with the job and do something. People do not want this stuff. The only time in my parliamentary career that I regret we do not have television here is this afternoon, because it would be illuminating if the people of Canada could see for once how time is wasted by the very people who are shedding crocodile tears all over the country about this government that has imposed closure, which it did not do. What it did was to impose time allocation.
I hope that in the next ten minutes some member of the opposition will talk some sense and will address himself more closely to the subject.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to intervene only briefly in the discussion this afternoon. I begin by congratulating the government for introducing these amendments which should go a long way toward meeting the requests of the co-operatives and credit unions of Canada. There is one aspect that amazes me, and that is why the government has taken so long in bringing forward its policies and why it has been so inconsistent. When I say inconsistent, I refer to the different attitude that was shown by the Department of Finance on the one hand in the bill which they introduced and, on the other hand, the activities of several other departments.
For years the Department of Fisheries encouraged marketing co-ops among fisherman and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development encouraged the development of co-ops in the north for various purposes. While this bill was being drafted that department was commemorating the establishment in my riding of the first credit union in North America, although at the time it was not called that. I believe this was a wise decision on the part of the National Historic Sites service, commemorating the establishment of The Farmers' Bank of Rustico which is in my constituency. A plaque was placed on the building which still exists, and it reads as follows:
Under the leadership of Rev. G.-A. Belcourt, a former pioneer missionary in the West, his parishioners erected this building to house one of the first people's banks in Canada. Chartered in 1864, and directed by farmers and fishermen, it continued to operate until 1894 and foreshadowed the development of the credit union movement. The bank, by providing cheap credit, enabled the people of this predominantly Acadian community to gain economic independence.
These types of self-help organizations have been a very vital factor in my province and in fact in many parts of the Atlantic region over the years. It is fitting that that sort of self-help when it is exhibited by Canadians, in the form of banding together either in co-ops or credit unions, should be encouraged. I want to congratulate their national organizations, their regional organizations and their local organizations for the very excellent job they did, not in lobbying-because I think that term has connotations which are slightly derogatory-but in educating the Canadian people on what they were requesting and informing Members of Parliament of their objective view of the matter.
They wanted nothing but a fair competitive position with respect to other types of organizations. I think that the work done by co-ops and credit unions in informing Members of Parliament and the government was a very useful exercise, and I congratulate the government for finally reacting favourably to their submissions. I must admit that it is not very reassuring that it took the government so long to react favourably. If I were concerned with the life expectancy of the government, which at present seems to be rather short, I would suggest that it react more quickly and more sensitively to the wishes of the Canadian people with respect to changes in policy.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I think the amendments will meet the requirements of both the co-ops and credit unions in my province where they have done a great deal of good work over the years.

For 25 years we have been going down the wrong road and now the government seems prepared to change direction. This is something for which we should be profoundly thankful.
However, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to be fulsome in my praise of the government and say it was a sudden burst of enlightenment on its part that caused this change to be made. That does not represent the facts. There are members on the government side of the House, just as there are in all parties, who fought for the co-ops. maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was saying when the House adjourned at six o'clock that I think it is pretty important that we recognize how we got these amendments relating to co-operatives and credit unions. I believe that the credit must go to those organizations. In this House there were spokesmen who believed in and worked for amendments of this kind, but it was mainly the solid work of the co-operatives and credit union members and organizations outside this House that brought about the change.

I think it is important to understand what happened because in my view this is participatory democracy. I do not think any government by itself, no matter of what party, can do the job of governing without having counterpoise and counterweight from outside in the form of organizations to keep it informed and, if need be, to put pressure on it. I firmly believe this. The credit unions and co-operatives brought this pressure to bear on the government which did, in quite a proper manner, bring about the changes that were required. This is participatory democracy in the real sense. It is not people turning out to acclaim a leader or to admire images and that sort of thing; it is people who know what they want, who are well organized and bring pressure of the right sort on Parliament and the government in order to get the changes they need.
This is exactly what happened to bring about the changes in those sections of the bill relating to co-operatives and credit unions. I am very glad to see this happen, and far from being censorious of the government for having changed its mind, I think it deserves credit. When you get a government or individual who is afraid to change his mind, you have a dinosaur or something which is no longer in tune with the needs of the day. I think the government did the right thing in changing its mind. I am almost tempted to name the individuals who had a lot to do with changing it, but I will not.
These amendments mean that the government now definitely recognizes that co-operatives and credit unions are different from the ordinary run of private business. Some time ago I picked out an editorial from The Western Producer of September 30, 1971. This is a time-honoured organ of the Prairies. I should like to quote the editorial as follows:
There is a fundamental difference between a co-operative and a privately-owned enterprise: the co-operative principle means that member-patrons share earnings according to the extent of their patronage of their own business, but in the private corporation, earnings are paid out to shareholders, who may or may not have the slightest interest in the corporation in which they invest, beyond the collection of dividends on their shares.
The member of a co-operative, on the other hand, has interests in common with his fellow members. They set up their co-ops to provide themselves with goods and services at cost; they do not expect any return on whatever they have invested in their own business.
I think that is basically the difference and I am very glad that the government has recognized it. The co-operatives and credit unions are comprised of people working together to secure goods and services for themselves. The co-operative movement, whether it be through co-operatives or credit unions, is a way of living, a philosophy of life. In this House we worry a lot about poverty and low income groups, but I think the co-operative movement has done more for low income people than almost any other movement which can be mentioned-

-from the days of Father Tompkins in the maritime provinces and the friends of the fishermen. That university did tremendous work in eastern Canada and its students went overseas to help the underdeveloped

On the western plains the co-operatives have done tremendous work for farm people and have taught them rugged initiative and individual enterprise. If this government will recall its experience with its recent farm legislation it will realize that in western Canada it was up against a breed of people who had no intention of doing something just because somebody told them to do it. The co-operative movement had a good deal to do with teaching them to work together to serve the interests of their own group.
In England and Scotland the co-operative movement began with poor people, the 28 weavers who started it, and it moved into Scandinavia and other countries. In the underdeveloped parts of the world the movement is teaching people to work together as a group to achieve their own interests and not to pay toll to any other interests that stand between them and the things they need. I think the co-operative movement could play a very great role in North America. It could be a counterpoise to those great business corporations which are becoming larger and larger and more monopolistic as time goes on.
In Scandinavia co-operatives have been able to stand up to big corporations and compete with them in a way that other business competitors have never been able to do. I remember years ago visiting Sweden and seeing the Luma electric light factory. Previously only General Electric had been operating in the area. General Electric had been increasing the price of its light bulbs until finally the co-op stepped in and built the Luma electric light factory. Even while the factory walls were rising, General Electric cut the price of its light bulbs in an effort to deter the building of the factory. That did not work, and the result is that through the co-operative movement the people of Sweden have broken the monopoly of General Electric and are able to buy electric light bulbs for considerably less than they paid before the co-ops got busy.
That story has been repeated over and over again. That is why I want to end my remarks tonight by saying to the government that, far from scolding them for changing their mind, I am very glad they did so and that the co-operatives and credit unions have been able to bring this charge about with the help of people in all parties who believed in the necessity for change such as the co-ops wanted, and who believed in the co-operative and credit union movements. For these amendments the government will not need to apply closure. There will be no difficulty regarding passage; these sections will go through easily. As I say, the government was expecting too much if it thought we would pass these sections without taking time to hail them as a triumph for the co-operative and credit union movements of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take up only a few minutes of the time of the committee to say that I wholeheartedly approve of the amendments the President of the
Income Tax Act
Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) proposed to the bill we are studying tonight and which deal with the taxation of co-operatives and caisses populaires.
This afternoon, I heard several members of the opposition, notably of the Progressive Conservative party, say that the government has simply betrayed the co-operatives by equivocating.
Mr. Chairman, it seems those members did not understand the proposals of the co-operatives last summer, when they appeared before the Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in connection with the white paper on tax reform, as they probably did not understand either the amendments proposed by the government.
When the representatives of the co-operatives first came to testify, their original request referred to a withholding in the case of members receiving patronage dividends. The government rejected that proposal, because it thought-I agree with that as well as several other members-that the members of co-operatives who received patronage dividends for the purchase of consumer goods should not pay income tax on those patronage dividends. It is only as a result of discussions, specific proposals and serious studies by co-operatives and the Canadian Cooperative Council that an administrative formula was devised and that it was agreed, in accordance with statistics for the last few years, that a tax would only be levied when the patronage dividend would be over $100, so that only the members of co-operatives who would receive such patronage dividends, to be deducted from expenditures already claimed for income tax purposes, would pay income tax.
The opposition members-particularly those of the Progressive Conservative Party, including the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) and the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald)-who said that this afternoon did not seem to fathom the consequences of the first proposal by co-operatives, and probably not these either.
I wish to thank the government for introducing these amendments, thus showing it understands and appreciates the benefits the co-operative system and caisses populaires bring the country. Several times I spoke in the House of the social and economic implications of the co-operative movement in my riding, and I do not think it would be useful to state the arguments all over again. However, I would like to say that what the government did will have happy results in my riding where co-operatives are strong, not only because they enroll people in a certain socio-economic movement but because where they are active, mostly in the fishing sector and other industrial fields, producers obtain more for their goods. I think it is a recognized fact that wherever there are co-operatives, companies set their prices in accordance with the prices established by those co-operatives-which means that not only members of co-operatives, but all fishermen, benefit from it. The same phenomenon can be seen in the farming industry.
Before concluding, I would like to express my gratitude to members of the opposition, and particularly members of the New Democratic Party, who, I feel, have co-operated with the government during the debate on co-operatives in order to make sure that if the debate was to end with the application of Standing Order 75C, the amend-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I like all other members of the House received representations from credit unions in connection with this section of Bill C-259. When I began to receive these letters I felt it was my duty to meet with the credit union organizations in my riding because I must admit, as I freely admitted to them, that I am not as knowledgeable on this subject as I should be. One of the first things they pointed out in their attempt to educate me on this subject was the motto of credit unions-"Not for profit, not for charity, but for service." I believe this mottc clearly spells out their purpose.
A credit union is not a money-making or commercial organization. Many of them are small groups of individuals sometimes organized in a parish or a church. In many cases it is a group within a manufacturing or commercial establishment which has banded together. It is a form of mutual aid which has grown to a social force. We have heard some hon. members tell the House how they, as
Income Tax Act
members of credit unions, have been enabled to buy implements to start them off as young farmers. I know of men who through their membership in a credit union have been able to acquire sufficient capital to make a start in buying a home.
I know of another case where a man was able to obtain far more desirable employment simply because money loaned to him by his credit union enabled him to buy a car to provide suitable transportation. Credit unions, even the larger ones, have a humanitarian aspect to their operations which is often absent when dealing with the strictly commercial organizations. They fill a definite need.
A credit union is a classic example of man helping man, not through charity but through co-operation one man with another. It is a form of brotherhood. Because credit unions faithfully played a part and have been instrumental in the creation and development of opportunities as well as providing the wherewithal for many to take advantage of opportunities, their membership has grown throughout Canada. In Ontario alone there are now over 1,400 credit unions in operation. But with this growth has come bigness, which has led to the need and development of central credit unions whose function, according to provincial legislation, is to act as the bankers for local credit unions and in this capacity they are the depositories of substantially all of the liquidity reserves of the locals. Centrals are bankers, too, for the operating bank accounts of the locals and in this capacity act as the clearing agents for the credit union movement which function is the means by which payment is effected for credit unions orders negotiated by banks and the cheques negotiated by the locals.
Coming back to the motto of the credit union movement, "Not for profit, not for charity, but for service," a good many of the credit unions in Ontario are operated by a group of voluntary helpers with minimum operating costs. The profits are then distributed through (a) patronage dividends, which really amounts to a reduction in the interest rate charged on the loans to members; (b) dividends-that is, interest-to members; (c) additions to reserve funds; (d) 20 per cent, in Ontario, of the net profits are set aside as a guaranteed fund established by statutory requirement by the government of Ontario.
The dividends issued to members are reported and tax collected through the issuing of T-5 forms. The only tax money, therefore, which the government is now seeking to obtain is the money set aside for reserves and the money set aside by statutory requirement in excess of that allowable under Bill C-259. According to information available to me, it has in the past rarely exceeded 20 per cent of the net profit of the union. This is the point which has been obscured by the discussion. In the House we are led to believe, not through any intention to deceive on the part of any hon. member, that credit unions do not pay taxes. In reality the amount not being taxed is the amount required by law to be put into reserves. The rest is paid through the members themselves in their private tax returns. Although there is a strong legal case for tax exemption, with supporting precedents, credit unions have interpreted the white paper and the tax act as pronouncements of government policy and have from the outset agreed to pay their fair share of taxation.

December 7, 1971
Income Tax Act
I return now to the social importance of credit unions and the part they play in the betterment of living for many people, and maintain that it is just too much to ask voluntary workers in small credit unions to administer the complicated taxation formulas proposed. I agree with many credit union men that it would mean the winding up of many credit unions throughout Canada. The law would be the master, not the servant.
I was not in the House yesterday when the amendments were made to the sections dealing with credit unions, but during the weekend I had an idea which I should like to put forward now. It is that the formula proposed in Bill C-259 with respect to credit unions be scrapped and in its place rules should be established whereby a credit union must allocate its profit to its members. Each member would receive a T-5 form reflecting his share of the profit, being the equivalent of interest on his deposit with the credit union, which he will include in his taxable income. The profit so allocated would be the profit after all allowable operating expenses and "patronage" dividends. Further allowance should be made with respect to such amounts as are required to set up a reserve to provide for anticipated uncollectable loans, such a reserve to be based on a reasonable percentage of loans outstanding. The remaining profit is the amount to be allocated to members.
This is substantially what is done by the amendments which were introduced in the committee yesterday. Interest on deposits are taxed at personal rates. Dividends on shares are also taxed at personal rates. The amount transferred to reserves because of statutory provisions will be generally taxed at 25 per cent. This is not an unreasonable tax rate. Really, the government has now considered credit unions as a true agent of the members of the Credit union and is dealing with them as such for taxation purposes. It is true that these new rules are somewhat complicated but I believe the complicated period will not last longer than a year. After that, the government's formula should be simple for all credit unions to follow.
In conclusion I should like, along with other hon. members, to compliment the credit union movement and cooperatives for the very sane and sensible way they presented their case to all members of this House and to commend the government for taking the steps it did in bringing in the necessary amendments to Bill C-259 as it affects them.

The Caisse populaire movement is extremely important for the labourer and the small wage earner. It is also important in many other respects. This committee has in its wisdom made some changes to the bill that I think benefit those who need protection, such as small investors who have dealings with co-operatives. Those who have to pay tax under the bill can well afford to do so, but I am happy to see that the small individual will benefit from the proposed deductions from his income tax.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, though I intend to be brief I would like to express my satisfaction about the amendments presented since yesterday. I am under the impression that I have been living one of the most pathetic days of my parliamentary career. In fact, in three and a half years I never witnessed a warmer climate than today when congratulations are coming from everywhere and when the minister is being commended whereas he was condemned not even two weeks ago. This demonstrates that the arguments raised a few days ago, the briefs submitted by various organizations and the speeches of members made the minister understand how important these changes are. In addition, I am glad to recognize the understanding and the broadness of mind of the minister who considered the arguments and the briefs in such a fair way and agreed, considering the turn of events to review his position and allow those organizations to enjoy a very special status considering their aims.
I believe it would be a waste of time to go over all the arguments heard last week during the day spent to ask those changes from the minister, but I cannot help saying how pleased I am to support such movements, considering their work, their achievements and the objective which they had in mind until now and which they can maintain in order to expand in the interest of thousands of citizens who believe in those co-operative movements, in the Desjardins movement and who, rightly so, have known fantastic results.
I was wondering a while ago why the government seemed to create a climate of anxiety during a few months. Was it necessary for us to wait so long for those movements to hear the good news they heard yesterday? Was it necessary for these organizations to make these representations which are always quite expensive? Fortunately, it is the results that count. These, I think, have been satisfactory. It appears from comments received from both the Desjardins movement and other such organizations, that the amendments introduced by the minister yesterday are quite acceptable. The responsible authorities of these institutions stated today that they were very happy about them.
I would have been derelict in my duty had I not acquainted the minister of my complete satisfaction in the hope that representations in the same vein will be made in the future with as much objectivity. It should be acknowledged that the briefs submitted were most unbiased and

very serious. I believe that this had much to do with the minister's decision and I hope that such realistic briefs will be submitted in the future to make the government understand the needs of the community. I think this is the way we will be able to obtain favorable answers for the organizations concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I will simply express the wish to see again great days like the one we had today because it seems that the climate which exists today could generate faith among the population..

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad the hon. member asked that question because it provides an opportunity for me to say something that otherwise you would rule out of order. If the hon. member and his colleague from Saskatoon-Humboldt learned anything from the Assiniboia by-election, they should have learned that three-quarters of the people in that constituency belong to a credit union, a co-operative or the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. One Liberal from Saskatchewan now is one too many.
I ask the parliamentary secretary why the original proposals in this tax bill were included in the first place. If all his colleagues are such ardent supporters and believers in the co-operative and credit union movement, why were these provisions put in the legislation in the first place?
After the issuance of the Carter commission report a campaign was launched by the Income Tax Foundation, which hon. members on the other side and in the official opposition know something about, to destroy and discredit the co-operative and credit union movement in this country. Much of what was in the original tax bill was in the promotion of that breed of cat. When one looks at the representations made to this government, to the cabinet and to the caucuses of this House prior to and since the bill was proposed, one finds it passing strange that there were no protests from the official opposition, from the government backbenchers and from independent members. There was not a word.
Let this be a lesson to everybody in this place that when there are organizations that are part and parcel of the movement of the people of our country, whatever section it might be, any government moves at its peril to destroy that. Thank goodness this government and the happy parliamentary secretary, who has a lucky football team, did this, because the fight would have had to go on.
Let us also learn that these amendments which the government brought in are to undo what an outfit like the Equitable Income Tax Foundation were party to, headed by one Cecil Lamonte who used to be head of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. He has some friends in this place. The membership of that outfit consists of the private grain trade and the private lumber industry. They have exerted all their efforts and hundreds of thousands of dollars to destroy the wheat pools and to destroy the consumer co-operatives which handle lumber and other hardware products. I did not hear a word on this from any member of the official opposition or from the back-

bench Liberals who today are so happy about these amendments.
If the parliamentary secretary did what I think would be perfectly proper, he would discriminate in favour of the co-operative and credit union movement. It is very possible that these amendments will mean less revenue for the Minister of Finance: it is possible, if not likely. I think this is very good. If there is any other way of doing something about the kind of activity of the corporate people in Canada who have been hiding in tax havens for years and have been making incomes without lifting a shovelful of dirt, so to speak, or doing a decent day's work out of which they paid no taxes, then it is about time we discriminated in favour of a sector of our economy that does do something for and about the needs of people in our system.

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext: What are you shovelling now?

maintopic: NEW AMENDMENTS IN FAVOUR OF CO-OPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
If the amendments of the parliamentary secretary do nothing else-and I hope they will-they will make it possible for the co-operatives and credit unions to become larger, more numerous and stronger, because if they do not then an area will be left in our economy into which the state will have to move. They play a necessary and needed role in our economy if for no other reason than that they serve as a check upon the private corporate interests in this country, if for no other reason than to show that those who talk about competition will have to do more than just talk a good fight; they will have to compete.
When the private grain trade says, "We give you as good a price for your non-Wheat Board grains in the elevators as the co-operative does," that is perfectly true-but it would not be true if the co-operatives were not there, as farmers learned through bitter experience for too many years. When I walk into my consumer co-operative and it costs me perhaps two cents a pound more for peanut butter than it does in the local private enterprise operation, there is a perfectly good reason for it, that is, that the private enterprise operation has some competition for a change and has had to reduce prices.
I hope that the amendments of the parliamentary secretary will mean that the government of Canada and this Parliament will discriminate, for a change, in this small way in favour of the co-operative and credit union movement. If this kind of co-operation arises again on another item of legislation, may I leave one further message for the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt. There is a way to bring in amendments as a result of representations and as a result of what Members of Parliament say, and there is a way to cease being stubborn and to do something that needs to be done in terms of the grains industry, and that includes the three prairie wheat pools and United Grain Growers who in my opinion should be the only ones handling grain in the three prairie provinces.
Let me conclude by saying that there has been a great deal of posing going on today. I do not apply this word personally to any individual member, but there have been many members in the House who have posed today. I have felt sad and disappointed with them on a personal basis because they are people of whom I am proud and of whom I think a great deal. Many of those who posed today were not here when we needed them earlier. Had they

The official spokesman with respect to co-operatives is the hon. member for Moncton, who was the first speaker on this issue when these sections were called. The hon. member for Moncton was put forward by our party as our spokesman and to indicate our party's position. Until that time my impression, on listening to the members of the NDP, was that they were confused and did not know which way to go. As a result of that they moved an amendment which I thought was a good one. I say this with all due kindness, far more in sorrow than in anger. Having disposed of the New Democratic Party I would now like to turn to the Liberal party, those mice who roared today for the first time.
Why was this amendment put forward, Mr. Chairman? It is very interesting. Just a few weeks ago, in fact on November 10, some correspondence passed between the Alberta Wheat Pool and the Minister of Finance. The Alberta Wheat Pool, aided and comforted by the Conser-
Income Tax Act
vative party, the official opposition, was attempting to secure certain amendments to the legislation. Knowing they had our support, the members of the Alberta Wheat Pool had been in communication both verbally and through correspondence with the Minister of Finance. On November 10 the minister replied to the Alberta Wheat Pool and this is what his letter said in part:
The status of co-operatives was carefully considered during preparation of the tax reform bill. Originally these were small organizations, local in application, serving limited groups of people on a non-profit basis. However, many have now grown to a point where they compete with normal commercial enterprises while still benefiting from preferential tax treatment.
His letter concluded:
The government considers that the proposed new tax bill, as amended, will result in a fairer distribution of the tax burden while helping co-operatives in the transition from exempt to taxable status.
Some five or six months after this bill first came to the cabinet, and three or four months after it was first distributed to members of the House-I will not go into the issue of when members of this party received copies of it; hon. members opposite may have got theirs early but we did not get ours until September, and some hon. members opposite, judging from their speeches, still have not read it-the Minister of Finance gave his firm and considered opinion that there would be no change in the bill with respect to co-ops. This shows the value and the efficacy of parliamentary debate. There has been a great deal of loose talk tonight about who was responsible for these changes. COMBINES-INVESTIGATION OF SALE OF TORONTO "TELEGRAM" SUBSCRIPTION LIST TO TORONTO "STAR"-FEDERAL AID POLICY FOR CANADIAN PUBLICATIONS-PRESS REVIEW BOARD.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe we all agree that ideally the publishing of newspapers, magazines and books in Canada should be Canadian-owned as well as competitive and financially healthy. I also believe that Canadians today are more and more alarmed to hear that newspapers and publishing companies are going bankrupt or coming under foreign ownership or, even worse, developing into a monopoly.
In December, 1970, when the special committee of the Senate on the mass media reported to Parliament, 77 of 116 daily newspapers in Canada were already owned by newspaper chains or groups. The very recent sales of three independently owned Ontario dailies to newspaper chains have further increased this concentration of ownership. The three newspapers involved are the Belleville Intelligencer, sold to Thomson Newspapers Limited, and the Brantford Expositor and Windsor Star, sold to South-am Press Limited. In addition, it is believed that Southam Press is negotiating to purchase two other unidentified newspapers.
The decision of publisher John Bassett to stop printing on October 30 the 95-year old Toronto Telegram must have chilled the blood of many publishers across our country. Earlier today we learned that Thomson Newspapers Limited has bought the Cape Breton Post, Sydney's only daily newspaper. This purchase brings the number of Thomson newspapers in Canada to 32. This means that almost half of the daily newspaper circulation in Canada is owned and controlled by three chains, Southam Press, F. P. Publications and Thomson newspapers. The Desmarais group controls four of the nine dailies, plus 13 weeklies in Quebec and K. C. Irving has acquired all the English language dailies in New Brunswick.
What is most disturbing about this concentration of ownership is the fact that in less than five cities all the chain-owned newspapers are published in single newspa-

December 7, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
per towns. There is no local competitor to stimulate their enterprise in covering the news or to provide a diversity of opinion. We hear that dailies in Calgary, Winnipeg, Quebec City, Moncton and St. John's are apparently experiencing financial difficulties.
From available evidence it would appear that, given the competition from other news media such as radio and television, the advertising revenue available to the newspaper industry is often insufficient to support competition within a specific readership market. However, when a natural monopoly exists, such as only one newspaper in a city, there is a profit to be made. This being the case, many Canadians believe the public interest would be better served by an independent, locally oriented newspaper rather than a group, chain-owned newspaper.
If true competition cannot be sustained, then concentration of ownership must be avoided as much as possible because a combination of both circumstances may not always be in the public interest. A variety of forces have combined to produce a growing concentration of press ownership. Technology and economics may be the dominant force since they undoubtedly favour the development of increasingly large units of newspapers. But there are other factors also. These include laws and regulations involving income tax and succession duties and the apparent ineffectiveness of existing legislation governing mergers, trusts and monopolies.
It is desirable to study these factors deeply and as quickly as possible. Only seldom in recent Canadian experience has a newspaper merger come under official scrutiny. The Combines Investigation Act applies to products. Newspapers are a service industry. However, in 1957 the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission investigated the amalgamation of the Vancouver Sun with the Vancouver Province to form Pacific Press Limited and found that the merger did not constitute a restrictive monopoly but recommended that no further ownership change should be made without court approval. It also stated that a further decline in the number of independent dailies would be prejudicial to the public interest.
In view of the difficulties encountered by daily newspapers, the ethnic press, the church press and others, there is need for involvement by the federal government and its agencies to ensure that the Canadian press will be in a better position to serve the Canadian reading public in a better way. The federal government and other levels of government as well should take steps to preserve the existing independent papers by all proper means. Canadians are waiting impatiently for an announcement of a federal policy on Canadian publications.
In the formulation of this policy the government should give serious consideration to the recommendation of the Senate committee on mass media, such as a press ownership review board and a publications development loan fund.

Mr. Speaker, while I apologize for bringing the parliamentary secretary back to the House tonight I find that I must do so because of the difficulty in getting straightforward answers in the House or being able to continue a line of questioning to extract answers. Be that as it may, I am becoming increasingly concerned with the evasiveness of answers with regard to the government's proposal to increase family allowances under the family income security plan introduced in the House under Bill C-264. Last year, under the policy proposals indicated in the white paper on income security for Canadians, the government said:
It is expected that legislation will be introduced in Parliament early in 1971, so that the program may go into effect September,
1971.
As is my duty as a Member of Parliament, I sent notice of this good news to all my constituents, especially those who are in dire need of assistance in order to provide a few necessities for their children. I am sure that many other members did likewise. You can imagine my disappointment and that of many Canadians across the country when the government suddenly announced subsequently that in view of advice from various agencies the program would have to be revised to include families beyond the proposed cut off at the income level of $10,000.
However, giving the government the benefit of the doubt and knowing that even with all the expert advice they profess to have they can make mistakes, my faith was restored when they introduced Bill C-264 for first reading on September 13, 1971, and indicated that the target date for the repeal of the old act would be May 1,
1972.	The answers given to me to questions in the past few days, especially in view of the ambiguity regarding special agreements on social security with the province of Quebec, renew my suspicion that another delay may be in the offing and this worries me very much.
On one hand the Premier of Quebec expresses confidence that agreement will be reached, and on the other hand all I can extract from the minister and some of his colleagues is that discussions are ongoing. But I wonder if they realize that many hundreds of thousands of Canadian families in the low and no income brackets who depend on family allowances for extra food and clothing
December 7, 1971

for their children have been waiting since the 1940s for some show of sympathy and understanding of their needs.
It is very obvious, also, that in spite of tales of woe that the opposition are holding up the enactment of legislation, Bill C-264 could be introduced for second reading and passed with little or no delay-within a couple of days. Surely the bill could be completed in committee in another couple of sittings and third reading could be completed in another day or so. This would mean that if the government were really sincere in solving poverty in the country, since they are faced with massive unemployment, and if they are concerned about poverty stricken Canadians they would get immediate agreement from all opposition parties to pass the bill with the least possible delay.
In order to assure the people of Canada that the family income security plan will be dealt with, I ask the minister the following simple questions:
1.	In view of the hardships being experienced by many hundreds of thousands of poor Canadians, will the minister assure them on behalf of the government that they can expect increases in benefits as indicated in Bill C-264, on May 1, 1972?
2.	Does the decision as to putting into effect these increases depend upon the discussions with the province of Quebec and, if no agreement is reached, will it delay implementing the benefits to the other nine provinces?
3.	In view of the compounding unemployment situation which cannot be resolved, even with the many measures introduced by the government, can the minister say if the government will consider introducing Bill C-264 immediately with a view to having it passed as an emergency measure, and thereby enable the government to update the payment of family allowance increases as soon as possible, even before May 1, 1972?

Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to reassure the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe by telling him that he did not have to call me back in the House tonight because I spent the evening here listening to the speeches of my colleagues.
I have noted the questions which the hon. member has just put. In reply to his first question, I can say that that it is certainly the intention of the government to proceed as soon as possible with the implementation of the bill which will provide low income families with benefits far more substantial than at present.
As regards his second question, I would like to state that the discussions now taking place with the government of Quebec have certainly not delayed passage of this bill. I think that the hon. member is aware that the proceedings of the House are unfortunately slow and he will understand that the government would have wished to introduce this bill earlier. It has unfortunately been unable to do so by reason of the crowded agenda of the House.
As to his third question, I would like to state that the government would certainly like to give priority to this bill when the order of the day allows it to do so.
In any event, I think that the government's forthrightness cannot be challenged in terms of its desire to help

Canadian families and all Canadians increase their income. That the government wishes to combat poverty is obvious. On the one hand, it has acted quite quickly on the question of increasing old age pensions and granting additional income to senior citizens who have no other sources of income. It has considerably improved the unemployment insurance legislation and it proposes also to increase the benefits for large families, with low income.
I think that the hon. member should be commended for granting the government the benefit of the doubt when he said a few moments ago that he understood very well that it had intended to improve the bill by introducing certain amendments to the original proposal included in the white paper which was published two years ago. The amendments which were introduced between the time of publication of the white paper and the introduction of the bill by the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) are evidence that the bill has been substantially improved.

GRAIN-REQUEST FOR POLICY STATEMENT ON USE AND LEASING OF INTERIOR ELEVATOR FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this matter which is almost as much a question of privilege as it is one of simple discussion. On November 25, as recorded at page 9875 of Hansard, I asked this question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson):
Can the minister inform the House if and when bids were called for the purchase of the Canadian government interior elevator at Lethbridge? Will the minister also inform the House which grain company is acting as agent at the government elevator at Moose Jaw, and whether the elevator has been leased, is under contract, or under what terms it operates?
I did not get a proper answer to that question; Mr. Speaker called me to order. I asked again, with the permission of the Speaker:
Will the minister make a statement on motions in the near future informing the House what the policy of his department is, and indeed of the federal government, in regard to the use and leasing of interior grain facilities in western Canada, and explaining the basis upon which the grain will be handled in these facilities?
The Minister of Agriculture answered:
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think so, but I would be very happy to answer the hon. member's question if it is put on the order paper, and perhaps to expand on it a little.
These questions arose in the miscellaneous estimates committee and some questions I put to the deputy minister as to what arrangements they were making regarding the contract for these elevators. I could not get a straight answer from the deputy minister. He said that he believed it was a written agreement. I asked if it was an agreement between Pioneer Grain and the Board of Grain Commissioners and he replied that he could not speak on behalf of the Wheat Board and Pioneer Grain. I asked a further question, and he replied:
No, but you asked for arrangements that the Wheat Board and Pioneer Grain had. I am making the reservation that I am not in a position to make any commitment in tabling such documents.
That was in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates on November 24, 1971, at page 44 of the report.

December 7, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
On November 19, Mr. Speaker, Pioneer Grain Company Limited sent a circular letter to all elevator managers of its company headed, "Re: Arrangements finalized for using Canadian government elevators at Moose Jaw and Saskatoon". This came from its head office at the Richardson Building, Lombard Place, Winnipeg, Manitoba. It outlined the arrangements and agreement reached with the elevators. The second paragraph reads as follows:
Producers who named Moose Jaw or Saskatoon as their primary or alternate delivery point can now haul grain on quotas authorized by the Canadian Wheat Board directly to the Canadian government elevator at either of the locations mentioned and make use of 5 i million bushels of space available at each of these grain handling facilities.
Yet the Minister of Agriculture who is responsible for the Board of Grain Commissioners refuses to answer a simple question about what is being done as to the disposition of these grain handling facilities. He refuses to say what sort of arrangements are available to other elevator companies. He also refuses to table in the House what are in effect the studies into grain handling in western Canada which have been made available, as I understand it, to the grains council, to the railroads and to other institutions. He does not make the information available to this House.
At the same time, a deal has been made with one grain company with headquarters in the Richardson building in Winnipeg to have handling facilities out of the interior terminals in Saskatchewan. Why the secrecy, Mr. Speaker? Why, when on November 19 the grain company was circularizing its agents in western Canada, could not the people responsible in this House answer a simple question put on November 24 and 25? Do they not know, or are they afraid to tell what they are doing?
I know that very recently they moved a trainload of grain directly out of the facilities in Saskatoon. I know they spent money upgrading the facilities so that grain could be delivered by truck. I am not opposed to this. I am merely saying that this House and the farmers of Saskatchewan should be advised of the policy of this government, what they are doing and how they are proposing to use these interior elevators which are paid for and operated by the taxpayers of this country. If they are paid for and operated by the taxpayers of this country, then I submit those taxpayers are entitled to know the manner and type of agreement which has been entered into under which these facilities are operated.
I am dumbfounded at the minister not being able to answer a simple question and give simple information to this House and preferring to say, as recorded at page 9875
of Hansard, "No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think so, but I would be very happy to answer the hon. member's question if it is put on the order paper." The minister should long ago have made a statement to the House on how these interior elevators were to be operated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, the question raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) cannot be all that simple, even though he might say it is. After all, it took him ten minutes to explain his point. As I listened to him it seemed that he took strong objection to the minister not answering his question and to the minister's suggestion on November 25 that the question be put on the order paper. When the minister said, "No, I do not think so," he was answering the part of the question in which the hon. member asked if the minister would make a statement on motions.
May I suggest to the hon. member that he follow the minister's recommendation, if he has not already done so, and put his request for more information on the order paper in the form of a question. Or he could write directly to the minister, if he has not done so already, and in that way perhaps learn a great deal about the whole matter.
May I now attempt to answer the questions the hon. member has raised at this time. According to my information, in the case of the elevator at Lethbridge there has been an offer to sell and bids were called for in the press on November 3, the bids closing at noon on November 26. Applications have been received and are under consideration pending a decision. As for the elevator in Moose Jaw, to answer the other points the hon. member raised a few moments ago, I am informed that our policy has not changed there and that the elevator still operates under the Canadian Grain Commission. It receives grain for the account of grain companies, as has been the standard practice for years. I do not know if anything has changed there recently.
The hon. member mentioned Pioneer Grain Company Limited and the agreement that company has entered into. That company, I suggest, is doing the same thing as any other company. It has entered into an agreement with the government for using limited facilities. It seems that that has been the practice for years and will very likely continue. After all, the commission is accepting deliveries of grain on behalf of grain companies. That has been the practice in the past; that is the practice now. As to whether the practice has changed, I am not informed. I suggest to the hon. member that if he wants a complete answer he should write to the minister. I am sure he would be pleased to give a proper and complete answer.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
